Will This Help Me?

You don't really know what some answer choices on the LSAT mean.

SKIP FOR NOW IF

Instructions

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS
Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

Abstract Answer Training Regimen exists to fix abstract language Translation problems.

Very often, students will simply skip over or gist abstract language in the answer choices because they don't understand the vocabulary in these answer choices and haven't taken the time to internalize what the complex sentence structuring means.

The Abstract Answer Training Regimen is the opportunity to permanently fix this issue and boost LR and RC accuracy.

How This Should Be Done

You can focus on the Abstract Answer Training Regimen and complete it in a week or less.

Or you can dedicate some time to the Abstract Answer Training Regimen each day for a longer period of time within a larger Routine plan. For instance, you may decide you want to dedicate 30 minutes per day to the Abstract Answer Training Regimen within the context of your larger Routine.

If you're completing the Abstract Answer Training Regimen within the context of a larger Routine, you can progress through the objectives in the Abstract Answer Training Regimen in order, splitting up the objectives between days since you're working with a shorter time span.

For example:

On the first day, memorize the Uncut Method Vocab List.

On the second day, start the Method Vocab Remix.

Whenever you complete the Method Vocab Remix, start the Method/Flaw/Argument Part Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet.

For as long as you're working on the Abstract Answer Training Regimen, continue highlighting words from your sections to add to your Vocab Tracker.

SHOW LESS
How to Move On

Once you complete all of the objectives in the Abstract Answer Training Regimen, and you are no longer intimidated by abstract language in the answer choices, you can eliminate this Routine from your schedule and return to the other Accuracy Fix Routines.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

TELL ELLEN
FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
What Problem Are We Solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.
